note: Manoeuvres that operators and agencies published themselves. This is the POSITIVE control for the detector in pipeline/orbit_events.py: the debris and spent-stage population is a free negative control -- objects that cannot burn, so every flag on one is wrong -- and this table is the other half, events that certainly happened at times somebody else recorded. A detector with a zero false-alarm rate and a zero detection rate is just a detector that never fires, and without both numbers there is no way to tell those apart.
curationPolicy: Hand-curated and hand-cited, deliberately, rather than scraped. A scraper across a dozen inconsistent operator sites is a maintenance liability, and this project has already been firewalled once by an upstream for retrying failed fetches. Twenty well-sourced events are worth more than a fragile pipeline, and this file is meant to be extended by hand. NOTHING here may be inferred: if a source publishes a date but no delta-v, the delta-v is null. Several agencies publish manoeuvre dates and never publish magnitudes, and a plausible-looking number in that slot would be a fabrication sitting inside the file whose entire job is to be the truth.
sourceConstraint: Compiled from agency and operator publications only. space-track.org and celestrak.org were not contacted: they are the rate-limited, legally-scoped upstreams, and everything needed from them is already on disk.
scoringNote: The archive holds the whole of 2024 from space-track's published bulk bundles plus live hourly capture from 2026-08-07, with a real gap between the two. Scorability is decided PER OBJECT against that object's own contiguous observation runs, not against the archive's global first and last epoch: an event inside the gap is one the archive cannot see, not one the detector missed, and pipeline/orbit_campaigns.score_ground_truth_with_coverage records it as pending. Entries dated inside 2024 score immediately; entries dated 2025 or 2026 wait for the back-fill to reach them or for live capture to catch up. That is why a 2024-dated entry is worth several of any other year.

bestSource.name: NASA Glenn PIMS ISS Handbook
bestSource.why: One PDF per ISS reboost, debris-avoidance manoeuvre and deboost, going back to 2010 and still being published. Each states the exact GMT ignition time, the burn duration, the delta-v in m/s and the altitude change in km -- and gives BOTH the flight-controller planned value and the value independently derived from the SAMS accelerometers on board. There is no better public positive control for an element-based manoeuvre detector, because the truth here was measured by an accelerometer rather than inferred from the same elements the detector is reading.

events.quote: NASA Glenn PIMS ISS Handbook entry 'Progress 87P Reboost 2024-04-26'.
events.note: Date from the handbook's own document title, which names the vehicle and the date. The magnitude is inside an image-only PDF this machine has no OCR for, so the delta-v is null rather than guessed -- a plausible-looking number in the file whose whole job is to be the truth would be the worst possible bug. Scorable for detection, not for agreement.

events.quote: It became possible to execute a single manoeuvre of 12.3 m/s. The manoeuvre started at 14:34 UTC and lasted for one hour. The satellite reentered at 18:46 UTC on the 28th July 2023 over Antarctica.
events.note: The world's first assisted re-entry of a satellite never designed for one. Also the best available illustration of scale: the same paper records that in routine operations no prograde in-plane manoeuvre had EVER exceeded 3 m/s, so the final burn was four times anything Aeolus had done in five years.

events.note: No delta-v is published by NASA for either burn. The altitude change is the total across both.

cadences.class: Crewed station in low Earth orbit
cadences.statement: Reboosts are typically scheduled once per month, holding an operational altitude band of 405 to 425 km.
cadences.quote: Current signed ISS altitude strategy is to maintain an operational altitude range between 405 and 425 km. Updated March 2025. Allows more operational flexibility during solar maximum where the previous strategy (416 +/- 2 km) was difficult to maintain with monthly reboosts. Reboosts are typically scheduled to be once per month.
cadences.teaching: The altitude band was widened in March 2025 specifically because solar maximum made the old one unholdable. That is a space-weather effect visible directly in an operational decision.

cadences.statement: Orbit control manoeuvres about once a week; the orbit is held inside an Earth-fixed tube tens of metres wide.
cadences.quote: Orbit control maneuvers are performed once a week. Orbit positioning control for Sentinel-1 is defined using an orbital Earth fixed tube, 60 m (RMS) wide in radius.
cadences.conflict: ESA's own eoPortal page gives 50 m rather than 60 m for the same tube. Both are ESA pages; the discrepancy is theirs and is recorded rather than resolved.

cadences.quote: Copernicus POD Regular Service Review GMV-CPOD3-RSR-0036, January to December 2025.
cadences.teaching: Roughly weekly for Sentinel-1 and roughly every two and a half weeks for Sentinel-2 and -3, from counts rather than from a policy statement.

cadences.statement: About two collision-avoidance manoeuvres per satellite per year across the fleet; about one every three months for the Sentinels.
cadences.quote: Each of ESA's Earth-orbiting satellites is conducting, on average, two collision avoidance manoeuvres per year. For the Sentinel satellites, it is more frequent, with around one manoeuvre every three months, and around once a month the predicted collision probability is high enough that the flight control team must be alerted.

cadences.statement: 6,873 manoeuvres from December 2021 to May 2022, and 13,612 from June to November 2022 -- about twelve per satellite per year at that time.
cadences.quote: SpaceX satellites performed 13,612 propulsive maneuvers over the reporting period, averaging approximately 12 maneuvers per satellite, per year. SpaceX satellites will maneuver when the probability of collision is greater than 1e-5, as opposed to the industry standard of 1e-4.
cadences.warning: Later Starlink figures -- rising to more than two hundred thousand per six months by 2026 -- are NOT a like-for-like series with these. SpaceX moved its manoeuvre threshold from 1e-4 to 1e-5 to 1e-6 to 3e-7 over the same period, so most of the growth is a change in what counts as a manoeuvre, not in what the satellites did. Hugh Lewis, quoted by Space.com, estimated about 25,000 for the December 2023 to May 2024 period had the threshold held constant, against a reported figure roughly twice that.

detectorCaveatFromESA.quote: A collision avoidance manoeuvre can look similar to an orbit control manoeuvre to maintain a specific ground-track. In the same way, the observed behaviour due to passivation of fluids at the end of life of a mission does not need to be different from the effects of an orbit control manoeuvre. The philosophy behind this document is to accept these limitations and not to risk over-interpreting the available data.
detectorCaveatFromESA.why: ESA's Space Debris Office, working with better data than this site has, says plainly that the manoeuvre TYPES cannot generally be told apart from catalogue observations. That is why pipeline/orbit_events.py classifies the physical signature -- in-plane, plane change, raise, lower -- and offers the possible operational reasons as an explicit list of alternatives rather than picking one. The distinction the physics supports is what the orbit did; the distinction it does not support is why.
